title: Our own bottom
hook: on the highest throne in the world, we still sit on our own bottom (Essays 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, when I dance, and your line was when I dance, I dance. Did one ordinary act get all of you, start to finish? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

A king climbs the steps to his throne. Velvet, gold, a crowd holding its breath. He turns, gathers his robes, and sits down. On what, exactly? Montaigne, near the very end of Of experience, answers with a joke. It's no use climbing up on stilts, he says, because on stilts we still have to walk with our own legs. And on the highest throne in the world, we are still sitting on our own bottom.
screen: `A KING CLIMBS TO HIS THRONE.` → `ON STILTS, OUR OWN LEGS.` → `ON THE THRONE, OUR OWN BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: First, the joke. It's a little rude, and that's the point. A throne is the grandest seat there is, and the body on it is the same ordinary body as everyone else's. Montaigne uses the laugh to puncture something: the idea that rank, title, or achievement lifts a person out of being human. Second, the stilts. The stilts are anything we use to seem taller: a job title, a following, an expensive coat, being right in an argument. Fine, he says, climb up. But you're still walking on your own legs, with their aches and limits. Nothing you stand on changes what you're standing with. Third, angels and beasts. In the same closing pages he warns about people who want to rise above the human, to escape from being a person altogether. Instead of turning into angels, he says, they turn into beasts. He's wary of any striving, however lofty, that despises the body and ordinary life. Readers differ on how far to take this: some hear it as a gentle check on pride, others as a reminder that the spiritual life is lived in a body, at a table, among people. Fourth, the laugh. Today's practice is to laugh at your own importance. Not with contempt. With relief. The pressure to be more than human is heavy, and Montaigne sets it down with one cheerful, slightly rude sentence. When you feel very important, or very small, the line works both ways. Everyone you meet is sitting on the same thing.
screen: `A THRONE, AN ORDINARY BODY.` · `STILTS STILL NEED YOUR LEGS.` · `NOT ANGELS, BUT BEASTS.` · `LAUGH AT YOUR OWN IMPORTANCE.` · then, large: `OUR OWN BOTTOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: laugh at your own importance, kindly. Sit, and actually feel what you're sitting on: the chair, the floor, your own weight settling down. Now bring to mind something you've been taking very seriously about yourself: a title, a reputation, a plan that has to go perfectly. Set it next to the plain fact of sitting here, in a body, like everyone else. Notice whether it weighs a little less. Breathe, and let your weight rest for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Our own bottom. Montaigne's cheerful reminder that no throne lifts anyone out of being human. Today's word.
Your line: my own bottom. Today, when you feel puffed up or put down, notice the chair under you and smile. Same seat as everyone. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that even on the highest throne we sit on our own bottom as a cheerful check on pride and a reminder that every life is lived in an ordinary body.

fork.setup: you've just been handed a grand title and a seat at the head of the table. what does Montaigne remind you?
options: you're now more than other people.
you're still sitting on your own bottom.
fork.reveal: he doesn't say refuse the seat. he says no throne, however high, lifts you out of being human, and he says it with a laugh.

trapdoor: what you thought: our own bottom is just a cheeky joke.
what it means: no rank or achievement lifts a person out of being an ordinary human body.
what a scholar hears: it sits in the closing pages of the Essays, beside his warning that would-be angels become beasts.
